hero.eyebrow: UX · XR · UX Writing, designing for how people actually behave
hero.body: Most products don't fail at launch. They fail quietly: at step three of checkout, on the second screen of onboarding, in the moment a user hesitates and leaves. I find that moment, work out why it happens, and design it away. I've shipped 70+ products across SaaS, e-commerce and real estate, in English and Arabic, on screens and in headsets.
hero.scrollHint: The reasoning is below. So is the proof.

paragraphs: Good design starts before the first frame in Figma. It starts with a question most teams skip: what is actually happening here?

When a checkout loses 60% of its users and everyone blames price, I watch the sessions. When new users get lost, I sit beside them and see exactly where they stall. When a brief says *make it delightful*, I ask what it needs to achieve, then design something I can defend with evidence.

My background in political science taught me to read systems: incentives, constraints, and why well-meant plans fail the same way twice. UX turned out to be the same discipline on a different surface.
polisci: Question the brief before answering it
ux: Personas built from data, not decoration
about.pivot: Flat screens taught me hierarchy, rhythm and restraint. XR asks for all of that, plus depth, distance and the human body. I completed IIT Delhi's Executive Programme in VR & AR (Grade A) because the next decade of interfaces won't sit inside a rectangle, and I intend to help design it.
about.noVibe: Teams bring me in for judgment as much as for screens. The work looks good, and the reasoning holds up in review.

work.blurb: Three projects, each told from problem to result.
work.closer: Every case study follows the same spine — context, research, constraints, process, outcome, and the part most designers skip: what I'd redo. Read one, and you'll know exactly how I think before you ever sit in a room with me.

xr.blurb: Every scene here was built from scratch in Unity and Blender and tested in a real headset. In spatial design, you only know something works once you're standing inside it. Comfort, scale, wayfinding and ambient UI are what separate an experience from a demo.
xr.caption: Final simulation, recorded in-headset. Unity · Blender · Meta Quest.
xr.soundNote: Sound is off by default. Good spatial design invites you in; it never startles.

bullets: Designed end-to-end web and mobile products across SaaS, e-commerce and real estate, all shipped live.
Cut checkout drop-off from 60% to 35% by tracing the real cause through journey mapping and A/B testing.
Built a 200+ component Figma design system, adopted org-wide, that shortened developer handoff and kept a fast-growing product consistent.
Turned usability findings into stakeholder-approved fixes in Agile/Scrum with PMs, engineers and clients.
Named Employee of the Month three times.
Ran an independent design practice for e-commerce and retail brands, from discovery to developer handoff.
Grounded every decision in research: personas, journey maps, wireframes, testing.
Delivered mobile-first, WCAG 2.1 AA-accessible interfaces across web and mobile.
Most clients returned or referred others, which is the most honest metric a freelancer has.

cards.title: The Checkout That Kept Losing People
cards.body: 60% of shoppers abandoned checkout, and the business blamed price. The research pointed somewhere else.

cards.title: 200 Components, One Language
cards.body: A product shipping faster than its interface could stay consistent. I built the system that let three teams speak one design language.

cards.title: Walking Inside the Interface
cards.body: Environments built from scratch and tested in-headset at IIT Delhi, where scale and comfort matter more than pixels.

uxWriting.body: The right sentence removes a support ticket. The wrong one loses a customer at the exact moment they were ready to commit. I write microcopy the way I design flows: for the user's next decision, not the brand's next adjective.

examples.label: Checkout fee disclosure
examples.before: Payment details — then, only after the card number, the fee appears.
examples.why: The fee stops being a betrayal and becomes part of the agreement.

examples.label: Error message
examples.after: We couldn't charge this card. Check the number, or try another one.
examples.why: It names what happened and what to do next, instead of dead-ending.

examples.label: Empty state
examples.after: No addresses yet. Add one and it'll be here when you check out.
examples.why: The context turns a dead end into a promise.
